Boston is the capital and largest city in Massachusetts, in Suffolk County. The city's Office of Neighborhood Services recognizes 23 neighborhoods, and your neighborhood affects how a house sells more than the city name does.

Part of the cityNeighborhoods
Downtown coreDowntown or Financial District, Beacon Hill, West End, North End, Chinatown, Bay Village
Central and waterfrontBack Bay, South End, Seaport District, South Boston, East Boston, Charlestown
West and southwestAllston, Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore, Mission Hill, Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, Hyde Park
SouthRoxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan

The city has 53 ZIP codes, so check the ZIP and the neighborhood on your assessment record instead of assuming they match.

Boston was settled in 1625 and became a city in 1822. More than two thirds of inner Boston's modern land did not exist at the founding. It was made by filling tidal areas. That history shows in the houses: Back Bay has single family homes and wooden and brick multi-family row houses, the South End Historic District is the largest surviving contiguous Victorian era neighborhood in the country, and downtown and South Boston mix low rise masonry buildings with modern towers.

If your house is in a historic district such as the South End, ask the city whether review rules apply to exterior work before you plan any repairs.

Boston is the most densely populated state capital in the country, at about 13,977 people per square mile of land. Around 1.2 million people may be inside city limits during work hours. For a seller, on-street parking, building access and noise are real selling points or objections, and buyers will ask about them on a walkthrough.

Boston has hot, humid summers and cold, stormy winters, with occasional periods of heavy snow. The freezing window runs from about November 9 to April 5. Winters can bring wide swings, and the immediate coast often sees rain where inland areas see snow. Expect buyers to ask about the roof, windows and heating.

Massachusetts assessors value property as of January 1 before the fiscal year. An owner who thinks the value is too high must first file an abatement application with the city's assessors, due on or before the due date of the first actual tax bill. In towns that bill quarterly that is generally February 1.

The Appellate Tax Board then hears appeals. It holds hearings at 100 Cambridge Street in Boston at Government Center, and often by video. Most single family hearings run one to two hours, and a case takes about four months to a year to reach a hearing.

Call the Boston Assessing Department for the current rate, to ask whether your home qualifies for the residential exemption, and to confirm your abatement deadline. Your actual bill states the due dates.

Boston is in Suffolk County, so your deed is recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. Massachusetts charges a deed excise tax when a deed is recorded. The neighboring Norfolk County registry lists $2.28 for each $500 of the price or fraction of it, and the same state statute applies in Suffolk County, so ask the Suffolk registry or your attorney for its fee schedule.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. You need a certificate of compliance from the local fire department. Schedule the inspection as soon as you have a closing date, and expect to pay a fee.
  • Attorney. When a lender is involved, an attorney has to take a real part in the closing, so most sales use a real estate attorney.
  • Home inspection. State regulation 760 CMR 74 stops sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning an offer on a waiver of the buyer's inspection.
  • Title systems. Most properties are recorded land, but some are registered land with a Land Court certificate.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth also runs a registry consumer notification service that emails you when a new document is recorded against your property. Sign up if you are selling an inherited home or one with a title question.

Many Boston houses have more than one unit. If yours does, ask the city's Inspectional Services Department whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and ask your attorney how existing leases transfer to a buyer.

A direct sale lets you skip showings while tenants stay in place. Cash Home Buyers buys Boston houses as they are, and you can compare our number with a listing price before you decide.

1. Find your latest tax bill and note its due dates and any exemption on it.
  2. Call the Assessing Department about your abatement deadline and the residential exemption.
  3. Confirm your neighborhood and ZIP on the assessment record.
  4. Schedule the fire department certificate once a closing date is set.
  5. Choose a real estate attorney and ask about the Suffolk registry fees.
  6. If tenants live there, gather the leases and ask Inspectional Services about rental registration.

With a traditional sale, a buyer's lender adds an appraisal and a loan approval to this list. A cash sale drops them, and the house is bought in its current condition.

faqs.q: How many neighborhoods does Boston have?
faqs.a: The city's Office of Neighborhood Services designates 23, including Back Bay, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, South Boston and the North End.
Suffolk County. Deeds for Boston property are recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Boston property tax assessment?
faqs.a: File an abatement application with the Boston assessors on or before the due date of your first actual tax bill. If it is denied or ignored, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell a Boston house?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the rules for a sale of a one or two family home.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Boston house that has tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask Inspectional Services whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and ask your attorney how the leases transfer to a buyer.
